standard.title: Causes of First Nations Civil Rights Campaigns Before 1965
standard.description: the causes of First Nations Australians' campaigns for rights and freedoms before 1965, such as discriminatory legislation and policies, the 1938 Day of Mourning and the Stolen Generations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the historical context of First Nations Australians' lives prior to and during the early 20th century, including the impact of colonial policies and the preconditions for civil rights campaigns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the causes of First Nations Australians' campaigns for rights and freedoms before 1965, including discriminatory legislation, the 1938 Day of Mourning, and the Stolen Generations.

nodes.label: Discriminatory legislation and policies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the political and societal conditions that drove First Nations Australians' campaigns for rights and freedoms, including discriminatory legislation and the policy of assimilation.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two discriminatory laws or policies affecting First Nations Australians and explain how each contributed to the need for civil rights campaigns.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the conditions driving civil rights campaigns: legal status at Commonwealth and state/territory levels (denial of citizenship rights, exclusion from the census, exemption certificates), segregation and treatment on missions, the policy of assimilation adopted in 1937 by the Aboriginal Welfare Conference of Commonwealth and State Authorities; explain how these conditions created the structural conditions for organised resistance.
wider: Compare the legal status of First Nations Australians at federal and state levels, examining how the patchwork of different state legislation created different conditions in different parts of Australia
Investigate the lived experience of mission life through personal accounts — examining how segregation, restrictions on movement and employment, and the removal of children operated in practice
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand the specific legal and institutional conditions that First Nations Australians were fighting against — the actual content of discriminatory legislation — cannot meaningfully evaluate the significance of specific reforms in K11 (what changed) or why K13 identifies continuing gaps.

response_modes.reason: Map the specific rights denied at different levels of government — federal, state, local — before asking students to explain the cumulative effect. The legal framework is complex but essential: students need to understand what 'not being counted in the census' or 'requiring a permit to leave a mission' actually meant in practice.

success_criteria: Identify at least two discriminatory laws or policies affecting First Nations Australians before 1965
Explain how the policy of assimilation, adopted in 1937, affected First Nations communities
Connect at least one specific law or policy to the need for organised civil rights campaigns

nodes.label: The 1938 Day of Mourning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the significance of the 1938 Day of Mourning in the campaigns of First Nations Australians for rights and freedoms.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the significance of 26 January 1938 as the context for the Day of Mourning and describe the national Indigenous rights meeting held that day.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the significance of the 1938 Day of Mourning: 26 January 1938 marking 150 years since the arrival of the First Fleet; the national Indigenous rights meeting organised by William Cooper, Jack Patten, Pearl Gibbs and others; the Citizens' Rights for Aborigines resolution; explain why the Day of Mourning was significant as an early organised national act of protest against Australia's sesquicentenary celebrations.
wider: Examine primary sources from the 1938 Day of Mourning — including the resolutions passed and newspaper coverage — analysing how the event was represented in First Nations and mainstream Australian press
Trace the long history of 26 January as a date of significance, examining how its meaning has been contested from 1938 to contemporary Invasion Day/Survival Day observances

response_modes.reason: The Day of Mourning is most effectively taught using the primary sources from the event itself alongside accounts of the sesquicentenary celebrations it contested. The contrast between the official celebrations and the protest meeting brings the significance of the date into sharp relief.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The 1938 Day of Mourning connects to contemporary debates about January 26 — making it a productive bridge between historical inquiry and current significance. It also demonstrates how the same date can be understood fundamentally differently depending on standpoint.
success_criteria: Explain why 26 January 1938 was chosen as the date for the Day of Mourning
Describe the national Indigenous rights meeting and the demands made at it
Explain what the Day of Mourning represents as a milestone in First Nations civil rights campaigns

nodes.label: The Stolen Generations and civil rights
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore accounts of the past experiences of First Nations Australians who were members of the Stolen Generations and explain how these experiences influenced the civil rights movement.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the policy of child removal that produced the Stolen Generations and explain how the experiences of Stolen Generations members influenced the civil rights movement.
nodes.typical_width: Explore accounts of the past experiences of First Nations Australians who were members of the Stolen Generations — the policy of forced removal of children from their families, the conditions in children's homes and on pastoral properties, the severing of cultural and family connections; explain how these experiences, and the growing public knowledge of them from the 1960s through to the 1997 Bringing Them Home report, influenced the civil rights movement from the 1960s to the present day.
wider: Examine personal accounts of Stolen Generations members alongside government records from the same period, analysing what each source type reveals that the other does not

Investigate the role of Stolen Generations experiences in driving specific civil rights campaigns — tracing how personal testimony became political evidence from the 1960s to the Bringing Them Home report

response_modes.reason: Personal testimony is a powerful source type that requires careful framing — students need to understand both its evidential value (first-hand experience) and its analytical context (the policy framework that produced these experiences). Structure the analysis to move from testimony to policy to civil rights impact.

success_criteria: Describe the policy of child removal that produced the Stolen Generations and explain its stated justification
Use at least one personal account to illustrate the experience of a Stolen Generations member
Explain how the experiences of the Stolen Generations influenced the civil rights movement, identifying at least one specific way these experiences drove civil rights action
